hint: The server didn't accept your SSH key. For GitHub: create a key with 'ssh-keygen -t ed25519', then add the contents of ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub under GitHub Settings > SSH keys.

Your system's Python is managed by your distro, so pip won't install into it. Make a virtual environment instead: 'python3 -m venv .venv', then '. .venv/bin/activate', then pip install again. For command-line apps, 'pipx install <name>' also works.
Installing or updating software needs admin rights. Put sudo in front, e.g. 'sudo apt install <name>'.
This needs admin rights. Put sudo in front of the command.
apt doesn't know that package name. Run 'sudo apt update' to refresh the package list, check the spelling, or search with 'apt search <name>'.
An earlier install got cut off. Fix it with: sudo dpkg --configure -a

match: is not in the sudoers file
hint: Your account isn't allowed to use sudo. Ask whoever manages this computer for admin rights.
This folder isn't a git project. cd into your project folder first, or run 'git init' to start one here.
Couldn't reach that address. Check your internet connection ('ping -c 3 google.com') and the spelling of the address.
Couldn't look up that address, which usually means no internet connection. Check your Wi-Fi or network, then try 'ping -c 3 google.com'.
Your computer isn't connected to a network right now. Check your Wi-Fi or cable.

npm couldn't write to a folder it needs, usually a system-wide folder that belongs to admin. Don't use sudo for npm. Instead, run 'mkdir -p ~/.npm-global' then 'npm config set prefix ~/.npm-global', and add 'export PATH=~/.npm-global/bin:$PATH' to your shell profile (~/.bashrc).
You don't have permission to do this. If it's a file, try 'chmod' to change its permissions, or run the command with 'sudo' if it truly needs admin rights (but be careful with sudo).
The file or path doesn't exist, or you mistyped it. Try 'ls' in the current directory to see what's actually there, or 'pwd' to confirm where you are.
The shell doesn't recognize that as a command. Check for typos, or the program may not be installed yet (try installing it with your package manager, e.g. 'sudo apt install <name>').
You tried to do something to a directory that only works on files (e.g. 'cat' or 'rm' without -r). Add -r if you meant to include the whole directory, or target a file inside it instead.
You tried to 'cd' into or treat something as a directory, but it's actually a file.
Something already exists at that path. If you're moving/copying, either remove the existing file first or choose a different destination name.
'rmdir' only removes empty directories. If you want to delete a directory and everything inside it, use 'rm -r' instead (double-check the path first - this is permanent).
The system is blocking this action, often due to ownership or system-level protections. 'sudo' might help if you're sure this is safe to do.
You gave the command more inputs than it expects. Check if a filename with spaces needs quotes around it, e.g. "my file.txt" instead of my file.txt.
The shell couldn't parse what you typed - often a missing quote, bracket, or semicolon. Check for unmatched quotes or parentheses.
This file isn't meant to be run directly as a command on this system (wrong architecture or not actually a program). Check what the file actually is with the 'file' command.
Something else currently has this file open/running. Close other programs using it, or wait and try again.
Something else is already using that network port. Stop the other process using it, or configure your program to use a different port.
Nothing is listening on the address/port you tried to connect to. Confirm the target service is running and the address/port are correct.
Your disk is full. Run 'df -h' to see usage, and 'du -sh *' in a directory to find what's taking up space.
The filesystem (or this specific mount) doesn't allow writes right now. It may need to be remounted read-write, or you may not have the right permissions.
The command got too many files at once. Use a more specific name pattern so it matches fewer files, or run 'find . -name "*.txt"' first to see what matches.

The program crashed because it tried to use memory it isn't allowed to touch. This is usually a bug in that program, not something you did. Try again, make sure you have the latest version ('<name> --version' shows yours), or report it to the program's maintainers.
Git won't push because the remote has commits you don't have yet. Run 'git pull' to bring them in, fix any conflicts, then 'git push' again.

The two branches don't share any history, usually because they were started separately. If you're sure they belong together, run 'git pull --allow-unrelated-histories' once. Otherwise, check you're in the right folder.
